list.label: Stress or feeling overwhelmed
list.opening: Draft: when demands build up, it can be hard to know where to begin. Feeling overwhelmed does not mean you have failed; it may be a sign that you need support, rest, or a more manageable plan.
tips: Pause and take a few slow breaths. Notice what is happening around you and what you need in this moment.
Write down what is on your mind. Choose one small, useful next step rather than trying to solve everything at once.
Break larger tasks into shorter sessions, and include meals, sleep, and breaks in your plan.
Talk with someone you trust, an academic adviser, or a university counsellor.
list.faith: Draft: you may find comfort in prayer, Scripture, or speaking with a trusted pastor or spiritual adviser. You could reflect on Jesus’ invitation to those who are weary in Matthew 11:28–30, or the encouragement to “carry each other’s burdens” in Galatians 6:2. Asking for help and taking time to rest can be part of caring for yourself.

list.label: Anxiety or constant worry
list.opening: Draft: anxiety can make future problems feel immediate and certain. You do not need to dismiss your worries or face them alone.
tips: Name what you are worried about. Ask yourself: “Is there one part of this I can act on today?”
Use a grounding exercise: notice five things you can see, four you can feel, and three you can hear.
Set aside a specific time to think through practical concerns, then return to the activity in front of you.
Speak with a counsellor or healthcare professional if anxiety continues, becomes hard to manage, or affects your sleep, studies, relationships, or daily life.
list.faith: Draft: you can bring your worries honestly into prayer, even if you do not feel calm straight away. Some people find Philippians 4:6–7 reassuring. Prayer may support you, and it can sit alongside counselling, healthcare, and other practical help.

list.label: Exam or study pressure
list.opening: Draft: exams matter, but they do not define your worth or determine your whole future. A steady, realistic approach is often more helpful than trying to study without rest.
tips: List the topics you need to cover and choose a clear, achievable goal for each study session.
Work in focused blocks and take short breaks. Review what you have learned rather than only rereading notes.
Protect your sleep, eat regularly, and give yourself time to reset.
Contact your lecturer, academic adviser, or student support service if you are falling behind or unsure how to prepare.
list.faith: Draft: you might pray for wisdom, focus, and courage as you prepare. Remember that your value is not measured by a grade. Faith can encourage you to do what you can while treating yourself with patience and care.

list.label: Questions about faith or doubt
list.opening: Draft: questions, uncertainty, or changes in belief can feel unsettling. You deserve space to explore them without being shamed or rushed into an answer.
tips: Give yourself permission to ask questions and notice what has prompted them.
Write down what you are wondering about, and what you need from a conversation.
Speak with someone thoughtful and trustworthy who will listen respectfully, whether that is a faith leader, counsellor, or another person you trust.
If your questions are connected to a painful experience, grief, or pressure from others, consider seeking support for that experience as well.
Join ALPHA. 😊
list.faith: Draft: you can bring uncertainty and difficult feelings into prayer. The Bible includes prayers of anguish and questioning, such as Psalm 13. Doubt does not make you undeserving of care, and you do not have to reach a conclusion before asking for support.

list.label: Feeling down
list.opening: Draft: everyone has difficult days, but persistent low mood can make everyday tasks feel heavy. You deserve support, whether or not you can identify a clear reason for feeling this way.
tips: Tell someone you trust how you have been feeling, and ask them to check in with you.
Choose one small act of care, such as eating something, taking a short walk, or replying to a supportive person.
Keep some gentle structure in your day, while allowing yourself time to rest.
If low mood lasts, worsens, or affects your daily life, contact a university counsellor or licensed mental health professional.
list.faith: Draft: you may find comfort in prayer, Scripture, or the presence of a trusted faith community. You do not need to hide how you feel or force yourself to appear positive. Spiritual support can accompany professional mental health care.

name.title: What’s the thought that’s weighing on you?
name.body: Write it the way it sounds in your head. It doesn’t have to be fair or tidy.
name.label: Your thought
examples: I failed this exam, so my whole future is ruined.
Nobody in my class actually likes me.
I have too much to do and I’ll never get it all done.
name.note: Nothing you type is saved or sent anywhere.

stepBack.title: Step back from it
stepBack.body: Read your thought slowly with these words in front of it.
stepBack.prefix2: I notice I’m having the thought that
stepBack.note: Notice what changed. The thought is still there, but you’re looking at it instead of looking through it. A thought is something your mind is saying. It isn’t automatically a fact.

knowGuess.title: What do you know, and what are you guessing?
knowGuess.body: Mark each part of your thought. Be honest: some parts may really be true.
knowGuess.moreLabel: Anything else you know for certain? (optional)
knowGuess.morePlaceholder: For example: I passed my last two exams. I still have the resit option.
knowGuess.allKnown: Okay. Even when something is true, how we tell the story about it matters. Let’s look at it the way a friend might.
knowGuess.guessOne: You marked 1 part as a guess. Predictions can feel certain, especially when we’re stressed, but they haven’t happened.
knowGuess.guessMany: You marked {n} parts as guesses. Predictions can feel certain, especially when we’re stressed, but they haven’t happened.

friend.title: What would you tell a friend?
friend.body: Imagine a close friend came to you and said:
friend.label: What would you say to them?
friend.placeholder: Speak to them the way you’d want to be spoken to.
friend.example: Draft: that sounds really hard, but it doesn’t make it the whole truth. What’s one thing that has gone okay lately?

balanced.title: A more balanced view
balanced.body: Draft: put what you know and what you’d tell a friend into one fairer sentence.
balanced.label: Your more balanced view
balanced.example: Draft: even though this feels heavy right now, I also know it isn’t the whole story.

nextStep.title: One small next step
nextStep.body: What’s the smallest useful thing you could do about this? Ideally something that takes five minutes or less.
nextStep.label: My next step
nextStep.placeholder: For example: message my tutor to ask about the resit
nextStep.example: Draft: send one message to someone I trust

summary.heading: Here’s what you untangled
summary.returns: Draft: the original thought may come back, and that’s normal. Nothing here is saved, so if it helps, write your balanced view down somewhere you’ll see it.
summary.help: If heavy thoughts keep coming back or are getting in the way of daily life, talking to a counsellor or someone you trust can really help.
